triage.name: Uterine Fibroids
triage.reason: Common benign uterine tumors presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure and bulk symptoms; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and pelvic ultrasound.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'pelvic ultrasound (transabdominal and transvaginal)' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']

demographics: Most common benign tumor of the female reproductive tract; present in a large share of women by the time of menopause, though many are asymptomatic
Black/African American women are affected more often, at younger ages, with larger fibroids and more severe symptoms
Symptomatic presentation is most common in the 30s and 40s, before menopause
Symptoms typically improve or resolve after menopause as hormone levels fall

risk_factors.text: Family history of uterine fibroids in a mother or sister
Increasing age through the reproductive years

comorbidities: Iron deficiency anemia from chronic heavy bleeding
family_history: Uterine fibroids in mother or sister

chief_complaints.text: My periods have gotten really heavy and last too long
I feel pressure and fullness in my lower belly
I have to pee all the time
My periods are much more painful than they used to be
We've been trying to get pregnant and it hasn't happened

hpi.onset: Gradual over months to years; often noticed when periods become heavier or a mass effect develops
hpi.duration: Usually present for many months by the time of diagnosis; may be an incidental finding
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; bleeding and pressure symptoms worsen as fibroids enlarge, and symptoms typically improve after menopause
hpi.location: Lower abdomen and pelvis; bleeding is uterine in origin
hpi.radiation: Pelvic or lower back pain may radiate to the sacrum, buttocks or thighs
hpi.quality: Heavy, sometimes clotted menstrual bleeding; pelvic pressure or fullness; dull, crampy pelvic pain
hpi.severity: Variable; bleeding can be heavy enough to cause anemia, and bulk symptoms can be moderate to severe
hpi.timing: Bleeding occurs with menses and may be prolonged; pressure and urinary symptoms are often constant and worse with a full bladder

associated_symptoms.text: Pelvic pressure or feeling of fullness
Urinary frequency or urgency from bladder compression
Constipation or tenesmus from rectal compression
Symptoms of anemia: fatigue, weakness, pallor
Abdominal distension or visible lower abdominal mass

pertinent_negatives: Severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting

atypical.how_it_differs: Fibroids may be asymptomatic or present with pelvic pain, and can be associated with miscarriage, preterm labor, malpresentation or obstructed labor; red degeneration can cause acute severe pain.
After menopause fibroids usually shrink and symptoms improve; new bleeding or growth in a postmenopausal woman raises concern for malignancy and requires evaluation.
Higher circulating estrogen from adipose tissue can promote fibroid growth, so fibroids may be larger and symptoms more pronounced at a younger age.

general.moderate: Well-appearing but uncomfortable; may show pallor of conjunctivae or palms from chronic blood loss
general.severe: Pale and fatigued-appearing, with signs of anemia or abdominal distension; may be uncomfortable lying flat
general.critical: Ill-appearing, markedly pale and tachycardic from severe anemia or acute hemorrhage; may be hypotensive

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae and mucous membranes
findings.finding: Conjunctival or mucosal pallor suggesting anemia from chronic heavy bleeding

findings.maneuver: Inspect the abdomen with the patient supine
findings.finding: Lower abdominal fullness or visible distension from a large fibroid uterus

findings.maneuver: Palpate the lower abdomen and suprapubic region

Mild lower abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs

findings.maneuver: Perform a bimanual pelvic exam to assess uterine size, shape and mobility
findings.finding: Enlarged, firm, irregular, non-tender uterus; size may correspond to a pregnancy of several weeks to several months
Nodular or irregular uterine contour from subserosal fibroids
Palpable adnexal mass separate from the uterus

findings.maneuver: Move the cervix side to side during the pelvic exam
Perform a speculum exam to inspect the cervix and vaginal vault
findings.finding: Normal-appearing cervix without lesions, discharge or bleeding; fibroids may occasionally be visible or felt as a cervical polyp or prolapsed mass

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam when a posterior mass or rectal compression is suspected
findings.finding: No rectal mass; the uterus may be felt anteriorly as a firm mass

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal and supraclavicular lymph nodes

Microcytic when iron deficiency develops from chronic blood loss.
Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can look falsely normal with inflammation.
Reactive thrombocytosis from chronic iron deficiency or inflammation.
Negative. Required in any reproductive-age woman with abnormal bleeding or pelvic mass before imaging and treatment.
Thyroid disease is a common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding and should be excluded.
Usually normal; a marked rise suggests an alternative diagnosis such as pelvic inflammatory disease or a degenerating fibroid.

Precise location and number of fibroids (submucosal, intramural, subserosal)

Distorted endometrial cavity

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Enlarged uterus with heterogeneous myometrial masses
Incidental finding when imaging is done for another reason
Coarse calcifications within the uterus

imaging.preferred_when: Abnormal uterine bleeding in a woman over 45, or any postmenopausal bleeding, to exclude endometrial cancer

initial.why: Excludes pregnancy, which changes the entire differential and management
Assesses anemia from chronic heavy menstrual bleeding
First-line imaging to confirm fibroids and map their size and location
Thyroid disease is a common reversible cause of abnormal uterine bleeding

confirmatory.test: MRI pelvis without and with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Clarifies atypical findings or maps fibroids before surgery or embolization
confirmatory.only_if: ultrasound is indeterminate, or surgery or uterine artery embolization is planned

confirmatory.why: Defines submucosal fibroids when heavy bleeding or infertility is the main problem
confirmatory.only_if: submucosal fibroid is suspected and ultrasound is inconclusive

supporting.why: Confirms iron deficiency as the cause of anemia

supporting.only_if: abnormal uterine bleeding in a woman over 45, or any postmenopausal bleeding

supporting.why: Directly visualizes and can treat submucosal fibroids
supporting.only_if: submucosal fibroid is suspected or hysteroscopic resection is planned

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for diagnosis; fibroids are usually an incidental finding and CT adds radiation without improving characterization
No role in evaluating fibroids; may be mildly elevated by fibroids and lead to unnecessary concern for ovarian cancer
Not part of the routine workup; normal fibroids do not cause significant inflammation
Not routine; consider only if a bleeding disorder is suspected from the history

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging and before any treatment in a reproductive-age woman
Pelvic ultrasound is the first-line study; MRI is reserved for indeterminate findings or surgical planning
Endometrial biopsy is required for abnormal uterine bleeding in women over 45 or any postmenopausal bleeding to exclude endometrial cancer
Rapidly enlarging mass, postmenopausal growth or postmenopausal bleeding should prompt evaluation for malignancy rather than assuming fibroids

differential.name: Adenomyosis
differential.why_considered: Heavy, painful periods with an enlarged, tender uterus in a reproductive-age woman

history: Severe dysmenorrhea that worsens over time
Symptoms often worsen in the days before menses
History of prior uterine surgery or cesarean delivery
exam: Diffusely enlarged, boggy and tender uterus
Uterus is typically symmetric rather than nodular
imaging: Diffuse heterogeneous myometrium without discrete well-circumscribed masses
Ultrasound may show a globular uterus with heterogeneous myometrium

differential.name: Endometrial cancer
differential.why_considered: Abnormal uterine bleeding in a woman over 45 or any postmenopausal bleeding, which can be attributed to fibroids
differential.trigger: Postmenopausal bleeding or abnormal uterine bleeding in a woman over 45

history: Bleeding between periods or after intercourse
Risk factors: obesity, diabetes, chronic unopposed estrogen, tamoxifen use
Weight loss or constitutional symptoms in advanced disease
exam: Uterus may be normal-sized or enlarged
Cervical or vaginal lesions may be visible
labs: No specific serum marker; CA 125 may be elevated in advanced disease
imaging: Endometrial thickening or mass on ultrasound
Endometrial biopsy showing hyperplasia or carcinoma
MRI for staging if malignancy is confirmed

differential.name: Ovarian cancer
differential.why_considered: Pelvic mass, bloating, urinary frequency and pelvic pressure that can mimic fibroid bulk symptoms
differential.trigger: Adnexal mass separate from the uterus, ascites, or persistent bloating with weight loss

history: Family history of breast or ovarian cancer
exam: Adnexal mass separate from the uterus
labs: Anemia or thrombocytosis in advanced disease
imaging: Complex adnexal mass with solid and cystic components

differential.name: Pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Amenorrhea, pelvic fullness and an enlarged uterus in a reproductive-age woman
differential.trigger: Any reproductive-age woman with abnormal bleeding or pelvic mass before imaging or treatment

exam: Uterus enlarged and soft, consistent with gestational age
imaging: Gestational sac, fetal pole or fetus on ultrasound

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding and lower abdominal tenderness in a sexually active woman

imaging: Thickened fallopian tubes or tubo-ovarian complex on ultrasound

differential.name: Ovarian torsion
differential.why_considered: Acute severe pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting in a woman with a pelvic mass
differential.trigger: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting

history: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral pain
exam: Peritoneal signs if necrosis has occurred
imaging: Enlarged ovary with reduced or absent Doppler flow

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Urinary frequency and urgency that can be attributed to fibroid bladder compression

history: Urgency and frequency with small voided volumes
exam: No enlarged uterus or pelvic mass
labs: Leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis
imaging: Normal uterus on pelvic ultrasound if obtained

severity.mild: Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic fibroids; normal or near-normal menstrual bleeding, no anemia, no significant bulk symptoms
severity.moderate: Symptomatic fibroids with heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, urinary frequency or dysmenorrhea; mild to moderate anemia may be present
severity.severe: Large or multiple fibroids causing marked bleeding with significant anemia, pronounced pelvic pressure or pain, urinary or bowel symptoms, or infertility
severity.critical: Life-threatening hemorrhage from fibroid-related bleeding with hemodynamic instability, or acute severe pain from fibroid degeneration or torsion of a pedunculated fibroid

red_flags.finding: Postmenopausal bleeding or new uterine growth after menopause
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for endometrial cancer rather than fibroids; requires endometrial biopsy
Suggests malignancy or another aggressive process; requires urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Heavy vaginal bleeding with hemodynamic instability
red_flags.meaning: Acute hemorrhage requiring emergent stabilization and transfusion

red_flags.finding: Severe acute pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Suggests fibroid degeneration, torsion of a pedunculated fibroid, or another acute process such as ovarian torsion

red_flags.finding: Fever with pelvic pain and tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests infected or degenerating fibroid, pelvic inflammatory disease, or another infectious process

red_flags.finding: Urinary retention or inability to void
red_flags.meaning: Large fibroid compressing the bladder outlet; requires urgent decompression

complications.name: Fibroid degeneration
clues: Heterogeneous signal within a fibroid on imaging

complications.name: Urinary retention or hydronephrosis
clues: Large pelvic fibroid compressing the bladder or ureters

complications.name: Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss
clues: Submucosal fibroid distorting the uterine cavity

complications.name: Preterm labor or malpresentation in pregnancy
clues: Large fibroid distorting the uterine cavity

special_populations.differences: Fibroids may be asymptomatic or cause pelvic pain, and are associated with miscarriage, preterm labor, malpresentation and obstructed labor; red degeneration can cause acute severe pain. Heavy menstrual bleeding is absent.
After menopause fibroids usually shrink and symptoms improve; new bleeding or growth in a postmenopausal woman raises concern for malignancy and requires endometrial biopsy.
Higher circulating estrogen from adipose tissue can promote fibroid growth, so fibroids may be larger and symptoms more pronounced at a younger age.

key_questions.question: How heavy are your periods, and how many days do they last?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, clots, soaking pads or tampons hourly, bleeding lasting more than 7 days

key_questions.question: Has your bleeding pattern changed over months to years, or is this new?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual worsening over months to years, consistent with slowly enlarging fibroids

key_questions.question: Do you feel pressure, fullness, or a mass in your lower belly?
key_questions.looking_for: Pelvic pressure or fullness from an enlarged fibroid uterus

key_questions.question: Are you urinating more often, or having trouble emptying your bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary frequency or urgency from bladder compression; retention suggests a large fibroid

key_questions.question: Are your periods more painful than they used to be?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysmenorrhea, which can occur with fibroids but is more prominent in adenomyosis

key_questions.question: Is sex painful?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspareunia from cervical or lower uterine fibroids

key_questions.question: Do you have lower back pain or constipation?
key_questions.looking_for: Bulk symptoms from a posterior fibroid compressing the sacrum or rectum

key_questions.question: Have you been feeling tired, weak, or short of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of iron deficiency anemia from chronic heavy bleeding

key_questions.question: When was your last period, and could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes pregnancy, which changes the differential and management

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble getting pregnant or had miscarriages?
key_questions.looking_for: Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss, especially with a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity

key_questions.question: Has your mother or sister had fibroids?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of uterine fibroids, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you had any bleeding after menopause, or bleeding between periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding, which raises concern for endometrial cancer rather than fibroids

key_questions.question: Has your belly been growing quickly, or have you had weight loss or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapidly enlarging mass or constitutional symptoms suggesting malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, vaginal discharge, or severe one-sided pelvic pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or discharge suggests infection; sudden severe unilateral pain suggests torsion or degeneration

key_questions.question: When did you start your periods, and have you ever been pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Early menarche before age 10 and nulliparity are risk factors for fibroids

reasoning_points: Reproductive-age woman with gradually worsening heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure
Pelvic exam shows an enlarged, firm, irregular, non-tender uterus consistent with a fibroid uterus
Pregnancy excluded with a negative hCG before imaging and treatment
Pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged heterogeneous uterus with well-circumscribed hypoechoic myometrial masses
Anemia and low ferritin explained by chronic heavy menstrual bleeding
Red flags for malignancy (postmenopausal bleeding, rapidly enlarging mass) are absent or have been evaluated with endometrial biopsy
Alternative causes of abnormal uterine bleeding such as thyroid disease and adenomyosis are considered and excluded

easy: Reproductive-age woman with classic heavy, prolonged periods and pelvic pressure
Bimanual exam reveals an enlarged, firm, irregular, non-tender uterus
Pelvic ultrasound confirms well-circumscribed hypoechoic myometrial masses
Mild anemia with low ferritin from chronic blood loss
medium: Patient presents mainly with urinary frequency or constipation rather than bleeding
Coexisting adenomyosis with a diffusely enlarged, tender uterus
Fibroids found incidentally on imaging done for another reason
Anemia is the presenting problem and the bleeding history must be elicited
hard: Postmenopausal woman with new bleeding or uterine growth, requiring endometrial biopsy to exclude cancer
Acute severe pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting from fibroid degeneration or torsion of a pedunculated fibroid
Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss as the only complaint, with a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity
Pregnant patient with pelvic pain and no heavy bleeding, where red degeneration must be distinguished from other acute causes
Adnexal mass separate from the uterus raising concern for ovarian cancer
